Codex</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Almost everyone at OpenAI has switched from ChatGPT to Codex to get their work done! When I asked Kathleen Chaykowski, who works in Comms at the company, she said she uses Codex far more than ChatGPT, including for drafting presentations, conducting research, and brainstorming strategies.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A separate notable detail in Andrew’s graph is that Engineering went from around 25% last September – when models had not yet significantly improved and Codex wasn’t as advanced – to 99% today.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>So, will non-engineering disciplines see equally rapid adoption of Codex-like tools, elsewhere? </span></strong><span>My sense is that the Codex team thinks the same will happen in other tech workplaces, so they’re preparing for a big increase in Codex usage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Zooming out to consider the question of external adoption of coding harnesses, it’s worth remembering that the AI labs I visited in San Francisco are not typical of companies in the wider economy in some ways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Selling AI tokens is the business.</span></strong><span> Everyone at these places is incentivized to use AI, learn about it, and get better at it. But this does not apply at companies in other sectors like retail, for example.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>No AI spending limits.</span></strong><span> Most companies do not have this luxury, while mid-sized-and-above tech companies are already capping AI usage in engineering. It’s hard to foresee such places doling out unlimited AI tokens to non-engineers!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>AI labs hire highly autonomous people. </span></strong><span>These places pay up to 50-100% above the top of the market, and attract folks with very high agency, who are extremely open to changing their workflows. Most workplaces are not like this.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So overall, I personally do expect non-engineering orgs to use tools like Codex, Claude Cowork, and similar ones a lot more, but not for them to hit 90%+ adoption within months. Nonetheless, visiting AI labs to learn about how they work is always valuable because I sense they’re months ahead of the rest of the industry in some key regards.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Will the main task of engineers be to make agents more efficient?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While visiting OpenAI, Anthropic, and Cursor, I took the chance to ask engineers how their jobs today are different from the recent past.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At Anthropic, Jarred Sumner, creator of Bun, told me something interesting: more and more of his work focuses on figuring out ways to make multiple agents “under him” more efficient. For example, he did a massive migration within the last two months that would normally take a year to complete. Instead, he spun up dozens of parallel agents that each took on parts of the migration.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>His challenge was to ensure the agents didn’t step on one another’s toes. He did not want to use Git worktrees because he found them too slow. He had all agents work on the same branch and divided the work so they would not touch the same file! Architecting so that agents can work in parallel took a lot of effort, and sounds like interesting, challenging engineering work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>This makes me wonder if software engineering could grow into a type of work focused on architecting in order for agents to execute better. </span></strong><span>A day after visiting Anthropic’s offices, I was at Cursor, where I asked the same question of cofounder, Sualeh Asif. He told me that software engineering will increasingly be about building the environment for agents to execute better.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And if we look back at the history of software engineering, it has always been about doing the highest-leverage work, while automating away low-leverage things. That’s why compiled languages became so popular because they automated away low-level machine instructions, and also why memory-safe languages became dominant by automating away memory management and errors. Now, we see the automating away of writing code: the next high-leverage work is setting up code architecture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I cannot speak for the industry, but it was interesting to see how development work is slowly shifting to “architecting the environment of agents” inside of AI labs. Of course, these places are building the platforms that run AI agents, and platform work is rarely the same as product work.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Still, as a software engineer, it could be worth experimenting with architecting for agent-type work. </span></strong><span>At the very least, it’s an interesting experiment from which insights can be learned about the constraints of today’s AI agents. Also, this skill could become in-demand in the future, so there’s an opportunity to get hands-on with it now!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Next trend: companies aggressively optimize spend per token?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When talking with engineers, a popular topic was token spend, and token </span><em><span>efficiency,</span></em><span> in particular. Another was GLM-5.2. Let’s start with that:</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Is GLM-5.2 the best & cheapest coding model?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GLM-5.2 is a new, open weight, free-to-use model from Chinese lab </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2cfc8161-94b5-4e67-a28b-f42f9641c7a0?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>z.AI</span></a><span> which is nearly as capable as Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, as per the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index – as we </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9e42c8b3-5f60-40c3-b267-9ec199038076?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>covered</span></a><span> two weeks ago. Or is it even better? The code security startup, Semgrep, found this open weight model does much better in cyber benchmarks than Opus 4.8. From </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8691a841-194e-4ce3-8ee8-951f21fc3479?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>their blog</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We ran a set of popular open-source models against our IDOR benchmark, the same dataset and the same prompt we’ve used to evaluate frontier coding agents. The result surprised us: GLM 5.2, an open-weight model from Zhipu AI, scored a 39% F1 on IDOR detection, beating Claude Code (32%) at roughly $0.17 per vulnerability found. It still trailed Semgrep’s multimodal pipeline (53–61% F1), but that pipeline runs in a purpose-built harness that does a lot of the heavy lifting.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Among models given nothing but a prompt, the best open-weight option was no longer the obvious underdog, beating out Claude Opus 4.8</span></strong><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>While we were running [this experiment] it we were genuinely shocked. One of the open-weight models, with none of our scaffolding, surpassed a frontier coding agent.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Of course, Anthropic has a more capable model, Fable, but access to that model has been currently blocked by a US government intervention. For cybersecurity use cases reasons, this new Chinese open weight model could be the single best choice for companies without access to Mythos-class models.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>GLM-5.2 is getting lots of interest thanks to its cheaper inference, a 1M context window, while offering Opus 4.8-level coding abilities. </span></strong><span>Here’s Maddison Kanna, software engineer at inference provider, Baseten, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dec4156b-49ef-4b0c-a5e4-63ea006daca5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>on</span></a><span> what they’re seeing:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Such a vibe shift happening right now. We’ve gotten nonstop requests from people who want to start using GLM-5.2. Incredible few weeks for open source models.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Philip Kiley, also at Baseten, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fd77272d-d495-482d-9a58-30e174f74c48?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explains</span></a><span> why GLM-5.2 is such a big deal:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“GLM-5.2 is the biggest news in open models since DeepSeek-R1.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s easy to see why. GLM-5.2 delivers comparable performance to GPT 5.5 and Opus 4.8 at a fraction of the cost, generally 70-80% less expensive on a pure token basis (use our calculator to estimate savings for your workload).”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>GLM-5.2 was released around when the White House decided to block flagship models from Anthropic and OpenAI for political reasons, </span></strong><span>and</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>the same </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1b158b0d-9f0c-4547-a924-bcefd0d4382e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>is now happening</span></a><span> with OpenAI’s GPT-5.6. So, we’re in a situation where Anthropic and OpenAI supposedly have better, more capable models than GLM-5.2, but they are not allowed to release them!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And as it just so happens, at around the same time, Chinese lab Z.ai – an academic spin-off lab founded in 2019 – released a state-of-the-art coding model which is free to use. Of course, “free” here involves paying for inference, but there’s no model licensing fee.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s a bit tricky to understand the economics of Z.ai releasing such a capable model for free, when training this model clearly presumably cost an enormous sum. Z.ai is subsidized in part by the Chinese state, so it’s worth asking if these capable open models are China’s attempt to stir up global competition and weaken the business models of rival US companies like OpenAI and Anthropic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Right now, as long as the US blocks models more advanced than Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5 from release, the most capable coding model is an open one from China. It’s predictable that companies everywhere will move their token spend there for cost reasons, if nothing else.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>“Token smart” not “token hard”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cutting back on AI spending is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a4397501-8365-4881-a5b5-22a4861fa6d6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>turning into</span></a><span> a mega-trend across the industry, as we </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a4397501-8365-4881-a5b5-22a4861fa6d6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>covered</span></a><span> a month ago. But I reckon we could be seeing a new, similarly large trend emerging: tech companies looking to make their token spend more efficient. Coinbase is an example of this. Last week, the company shared that, in the last two months, it cut its spending on tokens by roughly half, while using roughly the same number of tokens as before. Visualizing this:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Coinbase reduced its total token spend by nearly half in the last four months, without greatly reducing usage. Data source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/11ca8a3e-f3dc-49fd-916f-3092d6c2e0b1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Coinbase</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Senior staff engineer, Mark Landgrebe, built much of the infra behind these cost savings and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7db5c3c4-872c-4e27-b835-30a1a4adfc47?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explained</span></a><span> the big levers to save cost: routing, caching, and cheaper defaults:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Routing</span></strong><span>: Coinbase routes every LLM request behind its own gateway, which is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/769c5dbf-2a68-4089-89e0-197ad0b5581a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>LibreChat</span></a><span>. This LLM gateway has cross-provider failover, so, if one provider does not respond, the prompt is routed to another. It has sensitive data redaction built in, and logging, as well as cost control. It’s like an LLM control plane!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Cheaper default models</span></strong><span>: Coinbase is starting to experiment with defaulting to open weight models like GLM 5.2 and Kimi 2.7 through its LLM gateway. GLM 5.2 is cheaper to serve than Opus 4.8, while having similar coding efficiency.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Caching</span></strong><span>: when running longer tasks like a coding session, it’s a massive waste to send over the full (and growing!) context window to the LLM provider every time. Coinbase improved its routing layer so they went from 5% cache hits to 60%. Now, each request is charged for the </span><em><span>net new </span></em><span>tokens, and not the existing context window.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Wipe context when starting a new task: </span></strong><span>when starting a new task, the context is wiped clean, lowering the cost, avoiding “context rot”, and improving the prompt’s efficiency.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><strong><span>LLM costs are high enough at many companies that optimizing token spend is worthwhile. </span></strong><span>Coinbase employs around 1,000 software engineers, so it makes sense to invest at the infra level in a better routing and caching layer, alongside using the new GLM-5.2 model as the default.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div AuthKit gives you hosted auth, customizable UI, MFA, social login, session management, and a path to enterprise features like SSO and SCIM when you need them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Free up to 1 million MAUs.</span></p><p class="button-wrapper" data-attrs="{"url":"https://go.bytebytego.com/WorkOS_063026","text":"Try it now →","action":null,"class":null}" data-component-name="ButtonCreateButton" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: center;cursor: pointer;border-radius: 4px;"><a class="button primary" href="https://substack.com/redirect/36b396ca-4f9f-4376-baaa-efa566d2c8bd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="font-family: system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';display: inline-block;box-sizing: border-box;cursor: pointer;border: none;border-radius: 8px;font-size: 14px;line-height: 20px;font-weight: 600;text-align: center;margin: 0;opacity: 1;outline: none;white-space: nowrap;color: #ffffff !important;text-decoration: none !important;background-color: #7756e3;padding: 12px 20px;height: auto;"><span style="color: #ffffff;text-decoration: none;">Try it now →</span></a></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>What feels like a real-time conversation with AI today is built from many parts working together.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>At the center sits a language model that works in turns, the same way ChatGPT does when you type to it. The responsiveness comes from a layer of helper systems wrapped around that model, predicting when the user has paused, transcribing audio, generating speech from text, and weaving the pieces together fast enough that the conversation feels fluid.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>However, new research from Thinking Machines argues that this whole approach has a ceiling, and proposes a different way to build AI systems for real-time interaction.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines is a relatively new AI research lab focused on human-AI collaboration, publishing research under the name Connectionism and offering developer-facing products for the broader community. What sets them apart is the problem they have identified as central. Most AI labs treat autonomous capability as the most important capability to push forward, meaning the ability for a model to take a task, do the work on its own, and return a result.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines argues this framing sidelines humans. Real work, in their view, benefits from continuous collaboration where the human clarifies, redirects, and gives feedback as the model goes along. The interface should support that, rather than treating the human as someone who hands off a task and walks away.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will look at what the research preview covers and the concept of an interaction model proposed by Thinking Machines.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared </span></em><span>details</span><em><span> from the Thinking Machines Engineering Team. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Bottleneck</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The problem starts with how today’s models actually experience the world. A typical language model works in a single thread. It waits for the user to finish typing or speaking before it can perceive any input. Once the model starts generating a response, its perception freezes, and any new input gets queued for later.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines compares this setup to resolving a crucial disagreement over email rather than in person. The bandwidth is just too narrow. So much of what makes a collaboration work, the way your voice shifts when uncertain, the moment of realizing a direction change is needed mid-sentence, the reaction on your face when the other person says something useful, all of it gets stripped out of the channel between human and model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This matters because real work that benefits from another mind in the room depends on that bandwidth.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A model that only sees clean, finalized inputs forces a person to think like a model, preparing the full request, handing it over, and then waiting. In contrast, real collaboration is often messy, interruptive, and full of mid-stream corrections. Until the interface allows for that, the human ends up doing extra work to fit how the model wants to operate. Thinking Machines argues this bottleneck explains why much of today’s AI work feels like prompting and waiting rather than collaborating the way two people might.</span></p><div 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Harness</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If today’s voice AI feels real-time despite this limitation, how is that even working to a large extent? The answer is a pattern called a harness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A typical voice AI product is a stack of components glued together:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Voice activity detection listens for pauses and decides when the user has stopped speaking.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A speech-to-text model transcribes what was said.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A language model generates a text response.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A text-to-speech model converts that response back into audio.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A dialog manager orchestrates the entire pipeline so the latency feels acceptable.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Imagine a brilliant scholar who communicates only through letters slipped under a door. Making this feel like a conversation requires helpers. One stands outside listening for when the visitor stops talking, another reads the scholar’s letters aloud when they come back, and a third rings a bell when something visible happens that the scholar should know about.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The setup mostly works, but the scholar still experiences reality through letters. Voice tones, facial expressions, the moment itself, all of it stays beyond the scholar’s reach. This is what every real-time voice AI actually is, with a turn-based language model at the center surrounded by helpers that simulate conversation around it.</span></p><div justify"><span>Why does this approach have a ceiling?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It is because the helpers are simpler than the model itself. Voice activity detection runs on raw audio signals using a much smaller and lighter model than the language model behind it. This limits whole categories of behavior.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The system struggles with proactive interjections like “interrupt me when I say something wrong,” because the helper deciding when to speak operates purely on acoustic signals, while correctness remains the language model’s job. Visual reactions like “tell me when I’ve written a bug in my code” face the same problem, because the helper handles audio while anything on screen stays beyond its reach.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is where Thinking Machines points to an important lesson. As per a famous essay by Rich Sutton, methods leveraging general computation and learning consistently outperform methods that bake in human-designed heuristics. The same argument led from hand-crafted computer vision features to deep learning, and from hand-crafted game heuristics to self-play. Applied to interactivity, harness components are exactly the kind of hand-crafted heuristic that scale will eventually push out. The way past the ceiling is to put interactivity inside the model itself.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9c9122a2-1ebb-4441-a140-8c744fbbcdc4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">How engineering teams resolve incidents in minutes instead of hours. justify"><span>Three design choices stand behind this architecture:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first is time-aligned micro-turns, which change what the model treats as the unit of conversation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The second is an approach that skips heavy pretrained encoders, with audio and video going through lightweight processing components trained from scratch rather than being routed through standalone systems like Whisper.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The third is a two-model coordination scheme where a fast interaction model works alongside a slower background model that handles deeper reasoning.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines also did significant work on optimizing inference for this design, including contributing a streaming session feature back to the open-source SGLang library, enabling 200-millisecond chunks to be processed efficiently.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Micro-turns</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Most AI models work in turns, with the user speaking, then the model speaking, then the user speaking again. Each turn is a discrete unit, and the model processes one complete turn at a time. Even when a system handles audio, the underlying logic stays turn-based. The harness simulates real-time, but the model itself perceives the world in clear, separate chunks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines made a different choice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Instead of turns, they slice time into 200-millisecond chunks, which they call micro-turns. Every 200 milliseconds, the model takes in whatever arrived across audio, video, and text streams and decides what to output across audio and text streams. Time becomes the fundamental unit, replacing the turn entirely.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure justify"><span>This sounds like a small change, but it transforms what the model can do. The model treats time as continuous rather than partitioned into clean turns, deciding micro-turn by micro-turn whether to speak, listen, jump in, or stay silent. Input and output are happening continuously at the same time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Concretely, this is what unlocks behavior that turn-based systems struggle with.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The model can speak while listening, which is how live translation works.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>It can watch while speaking, which is how live sports commentary works.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>It can jump in mid-sentence when something visual happens, such as counting pushups in real time as someone exercises.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>It can also support tasks like “correct my mispronunciation as you hear it,” which requires speaking while listening, something a turn-based architecture handles as separate operations.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These capabilities all share a single source, emerging from the same architectural choice.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Coordination</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Time-aligned micro-turns solve responsiveness, but they create a new problem.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>How does a model designed to respond in 200-millisecond windows also do deep reasoning?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Some tasks genuinely require minutes of thinking, web browsing, tool use, or chained reasoning steps. Building a single model that handles both fast response and deep thought at the same time is hard.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines’ answer is to use two models working together:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The interaction model is fast, present, and handles real-time conversation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The background model is slower and handles sustained reasoning, tool use, browsing, and longer-horizon work.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>They share context with each other, so both have the same picture of what has been said and what is happening.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td justify"><span>`</span><span>The coordination works like this:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>When the interaction model encounters something that needs deeper reasoning, it sends a rich context package over to the background model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>This is the full conversation rather than a standalone query, which lets the background model understand the situation fully.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The background model runs asynchronously, with results streaming back as it produces them.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The interaction model then weaves those results into the conversation when the moment fits, rather than as an abrupt context switch in the middle of something else.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>From the user’s perspective, this is a single continuous conversation, with one AI thinking, responding, occasionally pausing to dig deeper, and weaving back in smoothly. Behind the scenes, two systems coordinate throughout.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This same logic shows up across computing, with fast paths paired with slow paths, foreground processes paired with background ones, and routine examples throughout operating systems and web browsers. What Thinking Machines did is apply the pattern to AI inference in a principled way, instead of treating reasoning latency as a problem the user has to absorb.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Capabilities</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>All of these design choices add up. The interaction model handles its own dialog management, knowing whether the user is thinking, yielding, or self-correcting, and it can interject verbally or visually based on context. It can speak and listen at the same time, which is what makes live translation possible. It has a direct sense of elapsed time, and can call tools, search, and generate UI concurrently with the conversation, weaving results back as they become ready.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These claims need evidence. Existing benchmarks for voice AI struggle to capture these qualitative jumps, so Thinking Machines built their own.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>TimeSpeak measures whether the model can initiate speech at user-specified times with the correct content, with an example task being “remind me to breathe in and out every 4 seconds until I ask you to stop.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>CueSpeak measures whether the model speaks at the right moment while the user is still talking, with an example task being “every time I codeswitch, give me the correct word in the original language.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>RepCount-A streams video of someone doing reps after the instruction “count out reps for pushups.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>ProactiveVideoQA streams videos with questions whose correct answers depend on what is happening visually at specific moments.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table justify"><span>The result is striking. Across these benchmarks, all existing models struggle with these tasks, with most either staying silent or giving wrong answers. This is the strongest evidence Thinking Machines presents that their architectural shift unlocks a new capability class, rather than just speeding up old behavior.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Limitations</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Despite the encouraging results, the research also points out the things that are still hard.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Long sessions remain a real challenge for this architecture. Continuous audio and video accumulate context very quickly. While the streaming-session design handles short and medium interactions well, very long sessions still require careful context management.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Connectivity remains a hard requirement, since streaming audio and video at low latency demands a reliable internet connection. A poor connection causes the experience to degrade significantly.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Scaling the model size is constrained by latency targets, with TML-Interaction-Small being the size it is, partly because Thinking Machines’ larger pretrained models are currently too slow to serve in this setting.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Looking back, the main argument is simple. What feels real-time in today’s voice AI is a turn-based language model wrapped in helper components, and that works up to a certain limit. Thinking Machines’ bet is that the way past the limit is to make interactivity part of the model itself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Two architectural choices carry most of the heavy work:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Time-aligned micro-turns slice time into 200-millisecond chunks, letting the model handle input and output as continuous streams.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The two-model split pairs a fast interaction model with a slower background model that handles deep reasoning, with both sharing context.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The evidence that this is a new capability class rather than just lower latency comes from the benchmarks Thinking Machines built themselves. Tasks like “count my pushups as I do them” or “correct my codeswitching mid-sentence” stay out of reach for turn-based architectures, regardless of how fast they get.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>An important takeaway is that adding a capability through external scaffolding creates a ceiling on how good that capability can get, with the scaffolding becoming the bottleneck rather than the underlying system. This pattern shows up across computing, and this research preview is one of the clearest recent illustrations of it in AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Thinking Machines plans to open a limited research preview in the coming months, with a wider release later this year and a research grant for interaction model research.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul item.title: The 80/20 Rule For Your Whole Life
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The 80/20 Rule For Your Whole Life

Yew Jin Lim

“The best investment framework isn’t the one that maximizes returns. The best career strategy isn’t the one that eliminates risk. The best contemplative practice isn’t the one that promises instant transformation. The best framework is the one you’ll stick with. For me, that’s been a boring foundation with a laboratory on top.”

#CareerGrowth
item.description: The 80/20 Rule For Your Whole Life

item.title: Three Bad Managers
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Three Bad Managers

Michael Lopp

“I worked for each of these humans. They either hired or promoted me. I worked for them for many years. As is my way, I’ve vastly altered the details of each human, but the core issue I describe is the core issue. Also, each of these humans is very smart. No dummies.”

#Leadership Management
item.description: Three Bad Managers

item.title: Cross-Team Pragmatics
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Cross-Team Pragmatics

Phil Calçado

“I’ve been in this industry for twenty-five years and have seen all sorts of companies and projects. You know what I have never heard? Someone saying, “You know what I really like about working here? Cross-team collaboration.””

#Leadership Communication
item.description: Cross-Team Pragmatics

item.title: How To Write An Effective Software Design Document
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

Michael Lynch

“I’ve written design docs as a developer at Google, Microsoft, and within my own companies. The specifics vary, but the underlying principles remain the same. A design doc should articulate the hard problems you’re solving and help your teammates give you feedback. Below, I share my approach to creating effective design docs and explain what belongs in a design doc and what does not.”

#KnowledgeManagement Guide
item.description: How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

Sumner Evans

“Even though it is used by a large number of popular open source projects, Conventional Commits is an actively bad standard which encourages focus on the wrong things and fails to deliver on its promises.”

#Tools+Setup

rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Even the most sophisticated AI agent in your stack starts every single message from a blank slate.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The model itself sees only the text placed in front of it at that exact moment, and the rest of the conversation lives outside its awareness entirely. Whatever continuity we feel when chatting with Claude or ChatGPT is something the surrounding platform is engineering on the model’s behalf, by inserting the right context back into every call. Once we understand this crucial distinction, the entire field of agent memory becomes a very different engineering problem from what it first appears to be.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will try to understand how that architecture gets built, from the constraint that forces it to exist all the way to the tradeoffs that follow.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared </span></em><span>details</span><em><span> from various sources. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Statelessness</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A call to a large language model follows a simple pattern. The system sends a prompt, the model returns a response, and the exchange concludes there. Each subsequent call, even one made a millisecond later, begins from a completely fresh slate. This is the API contract for every commercial LLM and reflects how transformers serve traffic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 justify"><span>When we say things like “Claude remembers our conversation from yesterday,” we are describing a property of the product rather than a property of the actual model itself. The platform writes things down on the model’s behalf, then reads them back into the prompt at exactly the right moment, so the model can reason as if it had been there all along. The intelligence resides within the model itself, while the memory resides in the system surrounding it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If the model itself works this way, the next question is whether we can solve the memory problem by writing everything into the model’s view on every call? The way this approach breaks gives us a better insight into how to solve this problem.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Context</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Every API call has a context window. It is basically the bounded slab of text that the model reads when generating its response. This includes the system prompt, the user’s current message, and anything else the developer has placed there. The model has full visibility into the contents of the window, while whatever sits outside it might as well live on a different machine.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: justify"><span>An obvious approach to memory involves writing the entire conversation history into the context window on every call. This works well for the first few turns of a chat. Once the conversation grows longer, however, three significant problems emerge at once:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first problem is cost. Every token in the context window is paid for on each call, in both money and latency, so a linearly growing conversation produces a linearly growing bill. By message eighty, the system might be re-sending tens of thousands of tokens on every turn just to maintain continuity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The second problem is latency. Larger contexts take longer to process, and a model that responds in two seconds on a short prompt may take ten or fifteen on one that has filled most of its window.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The third problem is the most counterintuitive of the three. The model’s attention degrades inside long contexts, and information placed in the middle of a long prompt is recalled less reliably than information at the beginning or the end. Researchers refer to this as the lost-in-the-middle effect.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background: rgb(0,0,0,.1);border: none;"></div><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Hierarchy</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Real production systems organize memory in tiers, each trading off speed of access, total capacity, and cost per token. The context window sits at the top, with progressively slower, larger, and cheaper stores below it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The analogy to operating system memory is evident. Modern agent memory systems draw heavily on the way operating systems page data between fast RAM and slower disk, promoting and demoting information as its relevance rises and falls.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A typical four-tier hierarchy starts with the context window at the top, fast and tightly bounded, with every token expensive at scale. Below it sits short-term or session memory, holding recent activity that has yet to be summarized or evicted. Beneath that is the long-term store, where persistent facts, embeddings, and structured summaries live across sessions. At the bottom is the cold archive, used for rarely-accessed material kept for audit or future reference.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" justify"><span>Information moves up and down this hierarchy as the agent works. A fact stated three sessions ago might be sitting in the long-term store, and the moment it becomes relevant, the system retrieves it and promotes it back into the context window. Conversely, when a session ends, the most useful parts of the context window get summarized and written down into the lower tiers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>ChatGPT’s memory feature uses a simple version of this idea. Stored user facts and summaries of recent conversations get prepended to every new prompt, while the current session occupies the working tier. The sophistication lies in what gets promoted to long-term memory in the first place, rather than in elaborate retrieval at read time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A hierarchy describes where memory lives. The kinds of memory we are storing are a separate question, organized along a different axis.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Types</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The field has converged on four functional categories of agent memory, drawing on concepts from cognitive science adapted for language model agents:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Working memory holds whatever sits in the live context window for the current task. For example, if the agent is helping us debug a function right now, the function code and our recent messages occupy working memory. The moment this task ends, working memory clears.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Episodic memory holds records of specific past interactions, anchored in time. A statement like “Three days ago, this user asked about onboarding new engineers, and we discussed checklist templates” represents an episodic memory, capturing a particular event with its context.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Semantic memory stores facts and knowledge that stand independent of any specific interaction. Statements like “Adam prefers Python over JavaScript” and “his team uses GitHub Actions for CI” function as semantic memories, surviving across sessions and applying wherever they are relevant.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Procedural memory captures learned ways of doing things. If the agent has figured out that this user prefers a three-section format for status updates, that preference becomes procedural memory, and the next time a status update is requested, the agent applies the format automatically.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 justify"><span>These four types are orthogonal to the hierarchy from the previous section.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A piece of semantic memory might live physically in the long-term store and get pulled into the context window the moment it becomes relevant. Most production agents implement at least three of these types, with the mix depending on what the agent is built to do. A customer support agent leans heavily on episodic and semantic memory, while a coding agent leans more on procedural memory. The right blend is a design choice rather than a fixed formula.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>All of this still leaves one important question open.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>How does the agent actually decide, on each turn, what to retrieve and place in the model’s view?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Storage can possibly be thought of as the easy half of agent memory. Writing a fact to a database or indexing a summary in a vector store are solved problems with mature tooling. The harder half is retrieval, which is the act of deciding on every new turn what belongs in the model’s awareness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Retrieval is hard because it requires judgment about relevance, and relevance shifts from one message to the next. For example, the user’s preference for Python matters when they are asking about a new project, while that same preference fades in importance when they are asking about pizza recipes. A good retrieval system surfaces relevant items at exactly the moment they are useful, and leaves the rest sitting quietly in storage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height:
