style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin: 8px 0;"><span>Use the code </span><strong>SCOOP</strong></p></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telecom companies are not short on AI ambition.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Across the industry, operators are talking about autonomous networks, AI-powered customer experience, predictive maintenance, energy optimization, fraud detection, AI-RAN, edge AI, and eventually 6G networks that are intelligent by design.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The vision is exciting. Instead of networks that mostly react to problems, telcos want networks that can sense what is happening, predict what might go wrong, recommend the best action, and eventually fix issues with little or no human intervention.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That sounds powerful.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But there is one uncomfortable problem hiding under all of this momentum: AI cannot do any of that if the data behind it is fragmented, delayed, ungoverned, or difficult to access.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is where telecom’s AI story gets complicated.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telcos are some of the most data-rich companies in the world. Every call, text, app session, roaming event, dropped connection, device movement, network fault, billing interaction, and customer complaint leaves a trail of information. The network is constantly producing signals.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But having a lot of data is not the same as being ready for AI.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For AI to work inside telecom operations, the data has to be available when needed. It has to be clean enough to trust. It has to be governed properly. It has to be connected across different systems. And in many cases, it has to be available in real time.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That is the real challenge.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Telco AI is moving from “nice to have” to network-critical</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the early stages, a lot of AI in telecom focused on safer use cases. Think customer service chatbots, sales support, marketing personalization, or back-office automation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Those still matter. But the industry is now moving toward a much bigger goal: using AI inside the network itself.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That includes things like predicting equipment failures before they happen, detecting congestion, optimizing energy use, improving service quality, identifying fraud, troubleshooting outages, and supporting autonomous network operations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is a different level of responsibility.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If an AI tool summarizes a customer support ticket incorrectly, that is a problem. But if an AI system makes a bad recommendation inside a live network environment, the consequences can be much bigger. It could affect service reliability, enterprise customers, emergency communications, regulatory compliance, or customer trust.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That is why telco AI needs a stronger foundation than ordinary enterprise AI.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It cannot simply rely on models that look smart in a demo. It needs trusted operational data, clear governance, strong guardrails, and real-time context.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">The problem is not that telcos lack data</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The funny thing is, telecom does not have a data shortage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It has almost the opposite problem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telcos have massive amounts of data sitting across radio access networks, core networks, transport networks, OSS and BSS platforms, billing systems, customer care systems, cybersecurity tools, edge environments, and cloud platforms.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The problem is that this data often lives in separate systems that were never designed to work together easily.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Some data is owned by network teams. Some sits with customer experience teams. Some is locked inside vendor-specific systems. Some is stored in legacy platforms. Some is too sensitive to move freely. Some is real-time, while some is only available after delays.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So when a telco says it wants AI to improve network operations, the first question should not be, “Which model should we use?”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The better question is, “Can the model actually access the right data, at the right time, with the right context and permission?”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In many cases, that is where the difficulty begins.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A predictive maintenance model may need equipment data, historical fault records, weather patterns, power usage, site information, and customer complaints. But if those datasets are scattered across different systems, the model may only see part of the picture.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A customer service AI may be able to answer billing questions, but if it cannot see live network conditions, it may fail to explain why a customer is experiencing slow service.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">An AI system may detect an anomaly, but if it cannot connect that anomaly to customer impact, service-level agreements, or recent configuration changes, it may not know what the problem actually means.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That is why fragmented data leads to shallow AI.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Real-time data changes everything</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For many industries, using yesterday’s data is good enough.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telecom is different.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Networks change constantly. Traffic moves. Devices roam. Cells become congested. Equipment fails. Demand spikes. Latency changes. Security threats appear. Customers complain in real time.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If AI is going to support network operations, it cannot rely only on old reports. It needs a live or near-live understanding of what is happening.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is especially important for autonomous networks.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">An autonomous network is not just a network with dashboards. It is a network that can observe conditions, interpret what is happening, and take or recommend action. For that to work, AI needs fresh data from across the network.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is why the industry is talking more about network digital twins, graph-based network views, edge inference, and real-time analytics.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A network digital twin, for example, gives operators a live or near-live representation of the network. Instead of looking at isolated metrics, teams can see how different parts of the network relate to each other. If something breaks, AI can use that connected view to help understand the root cause faster.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That is powerful, but it only works when the data is accurate, current, and connected.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Without that, a digital twin becomes just another fancy map.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Governance is what makes AI trustworthy</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There is another piece that does not always get enough attention: governance.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In telecom, governance is not just a legal or compliance checklist. It is part of the technical architecture.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If an AI system is helping make network decisions, operators need to know where the data came from, who has access to it, how it was used, whether it is accurate, and what the AI is allowed to do with it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This matters because telecom data can be highly sensitive. It can involve subscriber information, location-related data, enterprise traffic, infrastructure data, and operational security signals.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telcos cannot treat this casually.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A model that touches customer data needs privacy controls. A model that touches network operations needs audit trails. A model that recommends network actions needs policy boundaries. A model that operates across regions needs to respect data residency and sovereignty rules.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And if something goes wrong, the operator needs to answer very practical questions.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">What data did the model use?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Why did it make that recommendation?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Who approved the action?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Can we reverse it?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Was the data corrupted?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Did the model drift?</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Was the policy followed?</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If those questions cannot be answered, trust breaks down.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And when trust breaks down, AI does not scale.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Engineers will not rely on automation they cannot explain. Regulators will not accept systems that cannot be audited. Business leaders will not keep funding pilots that cannot move safely into production.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Why many telco AI pilots get stuck</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is why telecom AI often looks promising in pilot mode but becomes difficult in real operations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">A pilot can be controlled. The dataset can be cleaned in advance. The use case can be narrow. The environment can be simplified. The team can manually work around missing data.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Production is different.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In production, the AI system has to deal with messy data, changing network conditions, multiple vendors, real customers, real outages, privacy rules, security risks, and operational accountability.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That is where the cracks show.</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The model works in one region but fails in another.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The AI tool identifies a fault but cannot explain the business impact.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The system recommends an action, but engineers do not trust it.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The chatbot gives a customer a generic answer because it cannot access real-time network status.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">The analytics team builds something impressive, but the operations team cannot deploy it safely.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">These are not just AI problems. They are data readiness problems.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Telcos need a stronger data foundation</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If telecom companies want AI to move beyond pilots, they need to treat data as core network infrastructure.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">That means building a foundation where data is not just stored, but made usable.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telcos need to know what data they have, where it lives, who owns it, how clean it is, how sensitive it is, and which AI systems are allowed to use it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They need data catalogs, lineage, quality checks, access controls, streaming pipelines, and common data models. They need to connect network data with customer data, service data, infrastructure data, and business context.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They also need hybrid AI architectures.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Not every telco AI workload belongs in the public cloud. Some workloads need to stay close to the network because of latency, cost, privacy, or regulatory concerns. Others can run in private cloud, edge environments, or on-prem systems.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The future will likely be hybrid. AI will need to run wherever the data and operational requirements make the most sense.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In simple terms: telcos need to bring AI closer to the data, not always force the data to move toward AI.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">The winners will be the operators that make data usable</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The telcos that solve this first will have a real advantage.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They will be able to use AI to detect issues earlier, reduce downtime, lower energy consumption, improve customer experience, speed up troubleshooting, and create new enterprise services around edge AI and secure connectivity.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They will also be better positioned for the shift toward 6G, where intelligence is expected to become more deeply embedded into the network itself.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But operators that do not fix their data foundation may face a different reality.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">They may continue announcing AI strategies, launching pilots, and testing new tools, but struggle to turn those projects into daily operational value. Over time, the gap between AI-ready telcos and data-fragmented telcos will become harder to close.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is the real risk.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The future of telecom AI will not be decided only by who has the most models, the biggest budget, or the strongest vendor partnerships.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It will be decided by who has the cleanest, most accessible, most governed, and most real-time data foundation.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Bottom line</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Telecom AI is not failing because the industry lacks ambition.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The ambition is clearly there.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The real risk is that telcos are trying to build intelligent networks on top of disconnected data systems.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">AI cannot optimize a network it cannot fully see. It cannot automate decisions if the data is delayed. It cannot be trusted if the data is ungoverned. And it cannot scale if every use case requires teams to manually stitch together information from different systems.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">For telcos, governed real-time data is no longer a back-office concern. It is becoming the foundation of AI-native operations.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Without it, telecom AI will remain a collection of promising pilots.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">With it, telcos have a real shot at building networks that are not only faster and more efficient, but intelligent enough to adapt, recover, and improve in real time.</p><div class="callout-block" data-callout="true" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;background-color: rgb(238,238,238);border-radius: 8px;margin: 32px 0;padding: 16px 32px;margin-bottom: 0;"><h2 style="font-family: 'SF Pro 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I’m obviously biased because I started coding almost 30 years ago and built decades of muscle memory on top of a terminal-centric workflow ever since. But I did try GUIs every once in a while, from Visual Basic, Visual Studio, to Atom, and now the latest Codex app.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The reason I stick with terminals is very simple. I keep my flow and focus best when my hands never leave the keyboard. Some GUIs let you do everything via keyboard shortcuts as well, but they’re very inconsistent about it, which makes it hard to build strong muscle memory.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Terminal Emulator</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The terminal emulator I’ve been using for many years is</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d28a4770-7603-4696-9509-4b813cc0d634?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span> WezTerm</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It’s the only terminal I’ve found that is highly performant, customizable, and works consistently even when I’m forced to use Windows. 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The CLI agent harnesses nowadays are quite commoditized, and you won’t really go wrong with any of them. Almost everything I share below works with any mainstream harness you can find.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In fact, I actually recommend avoiding the “fancy” gimmicks that only some agents have, such as auto-managed memory. They’re often designed to lock you into a particular vendor, when in reality you benefit a lot from being able to switch to whichever newer model works best, even if it comes from a different vendor. I try to keep my whole workflow agent-agnostic, so I have no switching cost. It’s far from clear which model will win in the end, and as a user, you’re in a much better position if you can work with any model available rather than being locked into one.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Neovim</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Neovim has been my primary editor for a long time, and it’s a critical part of staying fully keyboard-driven inside the terminal. You might ask, “But I use agents now. Why do I need an IDE?”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I use it to quickly examine the file system, review diffs, and make small edits when needed. A few plugins do most of the heavy lifting:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I don’t let my terminal emulator manage tabs, because I manage all my sessions, windows, tabs, and panes in tmux instead. It’s one of the most powerful primitives in my whole setup, and it unlocks a few things at once:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Splitting my terminal window into panes the way I like</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Driving the entire terminal experience from the keyboard</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Persisting the working sessions and layout</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Accessing the same session from my other devices (more on that later)</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A popular alternative is Zellij, but tmux has worked well enough that I haven’t switched. 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Basic Prompting</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>We’re now in the terminal, and the agent is waiting for instructions. All I have to do is write a prompt. Sounds easy, right?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Actually, how you write your prompts is one of the biggest levers on both the velocity of your work and the quality of the outcome. So let me share a few things that made a big difference for me.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Using Voice Input</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Typing was my primary input method for decades. But over the last couple of years, speech recognition models have really changed the game. You can now run high-quality models locally on your Mac, for free, that generate output extremely fast.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>You talk a lot faster than you type, so moving to voice as your primary input is one of the easiest ways to greatly improve your productivity. It applies to prompting your agents, but also to anything else that used to require typing. This post, for example, is mostly written by voice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The solution I use is</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/88a3c673-77da-4586-ac31-721ca69d0953?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span> OpenSuperWhisper</span></a><span>, which is completely free and runs the Whisper model (turbo v3 large) locally. I set a hotkey to trigger it, and now I can just talk wherever I could type. There are plenty of other free and paid options that give a great experience as well.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Delegating like a Manager</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For many new tech leads and people managers, the first struggle is delegation. The same thing happens with how you interact with agents.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The most common mistakes I see people make about delegation to both humans and agents are:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>asking for an action, not an outcome;</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>not explaining the “why.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>taking back control.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Take “rename this variable.” It’s a valid prompt, but it has a couple of problems:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The agent finishes in a few seconds and waits for you again. It barely saves more time than doing it yourself, and you’re still the bottleneck.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>There’s no “why.” Do you want it renamed for readability? To follow a team convention? Because of a future plan you haven’t mentioned? Without the why, there’s no room for the agent to suggest something better, and it won’t know how to do it right next time.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If you were following a convention, a better prompt would be: “Let’s audit this part of our codebase and make sure our variable naming follows this convention <link_to_document>.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>That explains the rationale, gives the necessary context, and asks for an outcome instead of an action. The agent can run longer, get more done in a way that’s aligned with your goal, and respect that convention for the rest of the session instead of creating more problems for you.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The other failure mode is taking back control. When a mistake happens, people immediately think of doing it themselves. This happens to new tech leads working with a junior engineer. They could do the job faster by taking over, but in doing so, they make themselves the bottleneck and fail to scale. People hit the exact same wall with AI: they see an agent do something wrong and revert to doing it manually, and they never truly unlock the leverage agents offer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The right approach is to give feedback and help the other party improve. With agents, this is actually easier. You can write directly into the agent’s memory file (CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md), or ask the agent to reflect on its mistake and update that file so the same thing doesn’t happen again.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Planning Complex Work</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The feature I’m building right now is image input. I want the chat box in Hi Bit to accept a pasted image from the clipboard, or open a file picker or camera. This is a bit more than I think the agent can one-shot the way I want. In the beginning, I also didn’t know exactly where the button should go or what the attached images should look like.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This happens a lot: problems where I genuinely can’t describe the full solution up front. It could be a new project from scratch, a major refactor, or a big feature on an existing system. In those cases, I work with the agent to write a plan first.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>There’s a school of thought in the agentic community that’s against technical planning. They prefer to “just talk to your agent” instead.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I went the other way, and here’s why. When you just talk to your agent, you have to stay in an interactive session. You get constantly pulled back into the conversation, and after a few rounds, it’s hard to keep track of what the actual plan is. A long wall of text in the terminal is also painful to parse and hard to give targeted feedback on.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Instead, I spend a concentrated chunk of time up front getting the plan into a confident state, so I can hand it off for a fully autonomous implementation without jumping back in until it’s done. That’s also what frees me up to run other tasks in parallel without constant context switching.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For a long time, I did this by asking the agent to write a proposal in a markdown file, then questioning it and iterating. That worked, but I have something better now. Inspired by an article on using HTML as interactive artifacts, I built a tool called</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/93ebbef0-158e-4d01-adb9-5bbe283effa3?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span> Lavish Editor</span></a><span> to collaborate with the agent on anything complex.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>So instead of “draft a technical plan in a markdown file,” I say “draft a technical plan using npx lavish-axi.” Lavish guides the agent to render the plan as an interactive HTML page and opens it in my browser. It even encourages the agent to match the look and feel of the current project, so the plan for a UI feature looks visually consistent with the real app, which makes options far easier to judge.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" Being able to interact with a plan this richly, instead of editing a markdown file, turned out to be a big productivity boost, and it’s not limited to planning. I now use Lavish for brainstorming, reviewing changes, data reports, and anything else that benefits from a visual artifact and tight back-and-forth. It’s been a game-changer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Implementation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Once the plan is clear, the implementation is fully autonomous, and there’s honestly not much for me to do except wait for the agent to ping when it’s done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The one thing worth mentioning over here is that for every project, I spend a lot of effort making sure the agent can validate its own change end-to-end. As an example, for Hi Bit, I keep explicit instructions in the repo’s AGENTS.md for how to exercise the app, so changes like this get validated by the agent before they come back to me. I can often watch it test its own work in real time by driving the real app, attaching an image, and checking how the new button actually behaves.</span></p><div justify"><span>Occasionally, a task is so complex that it doesn’t fit well in a single context window. If I just let the agent grind on it, it fills its context, fires off very large requests, and eventually compacts to free space, sometimes losing important context in the process. The newer /goal command in Codex and Claude Code helps a bit, but I’ve been using something better since well before it existed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I call it </span><strong><span>good night, have fun</span></strong><span>: gnhf for short. It’s a dead-simple, long-running orchestrator I built for running big tasks overnight; you invoke it with gnhf <your objective>.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" justify"><span>Under the hood, it works similarly to the Ralph Loop and Autoresearch patterns. It breaks the task into small steps, and each step runs in a fresh context window seeded with a common base context plus the learnings from previous steps. Failed attempts roll back automatically, and the next attempt takes the failure into account. I can also set a token budget so I don’t wake up bankrupt. When I come back, there’s a branch with well-organized commits and a notes.md file summarizing what was done.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I reach for gnhf in three kinds of situations:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Implement a massive plan: gnhf “fully implement this plan…”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Improve a measurable metric such as reducing lines of code, increasing test coverage, cutting startup latency, or page load time: gnhf “improve <this metric> while keeping product functionality unchanged.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Run lots of offline experiments when you have an evaluator capable of scoring each attempt. For one project, I generated a game map by running 50+ layout experiments and scoring each through a gameplay simulation. Babysitting those by hand would have taken weeks.</span></p></li></ul><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Validation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Back to the image task: the agent has done the work, and it has produced a big change. Now what? This is where many people hit the real bottleneck: code review. There’s simply too much code to read, and reviewing it isn’t the fun part of the job.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I’m increasingly convinced that working with agents means acting like an engineering manager. Most managers rarely review code directly. They have the team review each other’s work, and before anything ships, they ask for evidence that it actually works. It’s the same with AI, except the developer is the manager and the agents are the team. You have to get good at using agents to scrutinize agents’ code, get them to self-correct, and get them to produce artifacts that demonstrate the feature really works.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I’ve experimented a lot here, and a few things turned out to matter most:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Run the reviewer agent in a fresh context window. If you review in the same session that wrote the code, the agent is biased by what it just did and assumes it was intended. It’s like asking someone to check their own work. They’ll catch some things, but it’s far weaker than a real peer review.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Escalate ambiguous, product-changing decisions to the human. Reviewers make mistakes, too. If you let the agent auto-fix every finding as if it’s all valid, it can drift into rabbit holes away from what you actually want. Keeping those decisions with the human keeps you in control of the ambiguity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Force end-to-end evidence. Today’s frontier models lean heavily on unit tests to validate changes, probably because of how they’re trained. But I’ve seen countless cases where every unit test passes, and the product is still buggy. You have to make the agent prove the change works E2E.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>I packaged all of this into an open-source tool I built called no-mistakes, which I now run on the image change. First, I use the neogit plugin to quickly scan the diff and make sure it’s roughly aligned with what I asked. Sometimes an agent goes in a completely wrong direction, and that’s obvious at a glance.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If it looks reasonable, I run </span><span data-color="rgb(24, 128, 56)" style="color: rgb(24, 128, 56);">no-mistakes -y</span><span> and it handles the rest: commit with a conventional message into a descriptively named branch, rebase onto the latest main and resolve conflicts, spin up agents to peer-review and self-correct obvious bugs, test the change E2E and produce evidence, close documentation gaps, fix linting, push, open a well-structured PR, and babysit CI until it’s green.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>All of it runs autonomously except for the decisions it deliberately escalates to me.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>This validation pipeline has become one of the most critical pieces of my whole workflow. My own stats show that 68% of the changes I pushed through the no-mistakes tool had bugs in them. I genuinely can’t imagine what my codebase would look like without it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Parallelization</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>With a fully autonomous implement-and-validate pipeline, a single task can take a while, and that’s a good thing, because it frees me up to run more things at once.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Handling Agent Status</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In tmux, this means opening a new window. Terminal tabs achieve the same parallelism. The important part is keeping those tabs visible and showing each agent’s status in the tab title. Claude Code and Codex do this out of the box; for harnesses that don’t, I wrote small plugins to do the same, and I made the </span><span data-color="rgb(24, 128, 56)" style="color: rgb(24, 128, 56);">no-mistakes</span><span> tool report its status as a custom title too.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>That one detail is what lets me run many sessions without going insane. At any moment, I can see which agents are running, which are done, and which need my input. A couple of tmux keystrokes jump me to any tab.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Managing Worktrees</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The other problem with running agents in parallel is that they step on each other’s toes when they share a directory.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Git worktrees exist to solve this. A worktree is an efficient clone of the same repo in another directory where you can work in parallel. But worktrees carry a lot of cognitive load: where to put them, how to name them, create a new one or reuse an old one, which are in use, which have dependencies installed, and whether env files are ready. What I actually want to think about is the work, not where to do it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>So I built another open-source tool named treehouse. You’re in a repo, you want to start a parallel task, you run treehouse, and it drops you into a ready worktree. Behind the scenes, it manages a pool of worktrees, tracks which are free, reuses an idle one when possible (so dependencies, build artifacts, and env files are already there), and makes sure it’s synced with the latest main before dropping you in. I don’t think about any of that. I simply run the treehouse tool and start working.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Remote Control</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Every couple of weeks, I have to drive my son to a birthday party, where I’d find myself useless for a few hours. He’d be having a great time with his friends while I sat somewhere with no Wi-Fi, missing my agents and wondering whether they were blocked and waiting on me.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>That stopped once I set up the remote control feature. I don’t use the built-in remote features from Claude Code or Codex for a few reasons:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>I want one consistent workflow across all my agents, not separate apps that do the same thing but stay siloed because different companies want to lock me in.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>I want real, full terminal access — not an agent-only view — so I can also run treehouse, no-mistakes, and gnhf.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>I want perfect continuity across phone, laptop, and PC. My son has zero patience: if he says it’s time to leave, I get up and go. If I typed half a sentence on my phone, I want to finish it on my PC later.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>So I set up</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb3b22cc-6a72-4d41-b226-c093ff4a24b8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: #7756e3;text-decoration: none;"><span> Tailscale</span></a><span>, which puts my PC, laptop, and phone on the same private network where they can reach each other safely. I then ssh between them (which on Mac just means enabling “Remote Login”). On my phone, I use an SSH client to connect to my Mac, attach to my tmux session, and instantly I’m in the same workspace with the same tabs, same agents, same environment.</span></p><div 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Putting Everything Together</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>So how does all of this come together on a normal day?</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>It usually starts with me talking instead of typing, describing a feature or a gnarly refactor by voice.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>If it’s complex, I have the agent draft a plan in Lavish Editor and iterate on it in the browser until it’s right.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Once the plan is solid, I either ask the agent to implement it directly or hand it to gnhf if it’s big, while I spin up a fresh worktree with treehouse and start the next task in a parallel tmux window.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>When an agent finishes, I don’t read massive diffs line by line. I run no-mistakes, which reviews the code, tests it end-to-end, and opens a clean PR while I move on.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>When I’m away from my Mac, I SSH in from my phone, and the whole workspace stays with me.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Here’s what the workflow looks like on a high level:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" style="mso-padding-alt: 1em 0 1.6em;"><tbody><tr><td style="text-align: center;"></td><td class="content" align="left" width="1456" style="text-align: center;"><a class="image-link" target="_blank" href="https://substack.com/redirect/37a92214-4b8d-42a9-ad2e-98e3df0433d5?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction: column;align-items: center;padding: 0;width: auto;height: auto;border: none;text-decoration: none;display: block;margin: 0;"><img class="wide-image" data-attrs="{"src":"https://substack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com/public/images/b5d3de4b-4180-4154-b4a2-cc22f67ffb24_2048x731.png","srcNoWatermark":null,"fullscreen":null,"imageSize":null,"height":520,"width":1456,"resizeWidth":null,"bytes":null,"alt":null,"title":null,"type":null,"href":null,"belowTheFold":true,"topImage":false,"internalRedirect":null,"isProcessing":false,"align":null,"offset":false}" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Each tool removes one specific point of friction, and together they chain into a smooth workflow I genuinely enjoy. I get to stay at the level of deciding what to build and whether it’s good, while most of what’s in between runs itself.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Closing Thoughts</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>That’s everything I can think of that made a meaningful difference in my workflow. Reflecting on how it came together over the past couple of years, my biggest realization is that as the models keep advancing, the tooling and workflow around them will keep evolving too. What works well today may be obsolete a few months from now.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>At the same time, relying only on off-the-shelf products like Claude Code and Codex is never quite enough. There’s always room for a better, more efficient workflow to take the agents a step further. I benefited a lot from building custom tools to remove whatever friction I hit. You’ll likely face a different set of problems because you work on different projects with different processes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;text-align: justify"><span>So I’d encourage you to never accept anything that slows you down. If part of your workflow frustrates you, chances are others are hitting the same thing. Find a tool that fixes it, or build one and share it. We’re in the middle of an industrial revolution. It’s the best time to be creative and redefine how things should work. Let’s tinker and have fun.</span></p></div></div><div class="postscript-placeholder" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><table Meta: “AI psychosis” in effect?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I thought it was a made-up story when I read that Meta had enabled account takeovers via a “zero auth” policy; i.e., simply asking the Meta AI bot was sufficient to change any account’s email address. After all, shipping such a regression would fly in the face of security measures, code reviews, automated testing, and metrics. Plus, the company has dedicated Integrity teams whose mission statement is to ensure something like this never happens… And yet, this bug shipped.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It went undetected by anyone at Meta, and high-profile accounts like that of former US president, Barack Obama, were taken over as a result. Instagram’s dedicated Integrity team seems to have discovered the embarrassing issue via the news.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As mentioned, it was two days before the Craft keynote, so there was enough time to ask around at Instagram and Meta. Engineers at the company there told me this disaster was caused by AI-generated, AI-reviewed code, along with layoffs, and by forced reassignments from Integrity teams and elsewhere onto AI labeling and related duties.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Integrity teams at WhatsApp </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/66a1e779-7ad2-4861-b344-e7ca60c1cdbd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Data labeling at the ADO group </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e027e955-db1a-40cb-b70f-179a25c5bb4f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>goes beyond</span></a><span> “just” labeling; there are many AI training tasks to do.  But these are repetitive, unless you get really creative.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Based on everything I heard from talking with Meta folks, AI-induced behavior was indeed at the heart of this outage. AI-generated, AI-reviewed code, and security teams being gutted, were also factors in the beyond-embarrassing incident. As reported in last week’s deepdive:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Instagram’s Trust and Safety Team lost around 50% of its staff to data labeling and layoffs. Some of the most senior folks were drafted onto AI training tasks.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>AI-generated changes with zero human input, with just an additional AI code review, have been very common in recent months across the codebase. The change that caused this outage looked like one of these</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Normally, the Trust and Safety team would be on top of monitoring and alerting of security breaches, but it is currently in full disarray due to rapid, internal disorganization”.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If major changes like data labeling assignments and staff tracking are undone, then perhaps things at Meta could return to normal. But so far, the most being done is that leadership has boosted budgets for snacks, travel, and events. Hardly the change needed to restore morale and the former culture!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The comparison to the Lumon warning</span></strong><span> about what happens when there’s so much focus on AI that the basic health of a company’s main – money-spinning – products is neglected. Instagram, WhatsApp, and Facebook generate the bulk of revenue for Meta, but the company is reallocating more engineers to training the coding model, and aggressively cutting the headcounts of vital orgs to do so – up to the point of not having oncall coverage for key services, and security teams being too stretched to do their jobs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Am I missing some insight about why it’s more important to build a state-of-the-art, likely-closed AI model that’s good at coding, than it is to keep operating revenue-generating businesses with stable infra?</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. Everything’s changed in six months</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Independent, experienced software engineers with zero affiliation to AI labs have been saying for a few months that how we do software engineering has been transformed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>David Heinemeier Hansson (DHH), creator of Ruby on Rails </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9f857e09-e344-48cf-95f9-78f193b7a3a1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in January</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>”Just [in] summer 2025, I spoke with Lex Fridman about not letting AI write any code directly, but it turns out part of this resistance was simply based on the models not being good enough at the time! I spent more time rewriting what it wrote, than if I’d done it from scratch. That has now flipped.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Simon Willison, creator of Django, </span><a 16px;"><strong><span>OpenAI: moving much faster with AI agents. </span></strong><span>OpenAI’s Codex team was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/76adcec9-db99-4850-acd7-7e6759d2de09?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>on the main stage</span></a><span> at The Pragmatic Summit in February. Tibo Sottiaux (head of engineering, Codex, OpenAI) shared interesting details on how software development is done in the Codex team:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>There’s a “fix this” button integrated into the internal OpenAI mobile app. It makes one-shot fixes to bug reports, which devs review and can merge</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>AI code review for all code changes. With a tiered approach, some changes can be merged with just AI review, and more important ones need an extra human review</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Most devs run several agents in parallel, often walking around with their laptop lids open, so the machine doesn’t enter sleep mode and suspend agents</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Code isn’t really written by hand anymore on the Codex team, and is also less common on other teams too</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>“Taste” is becoming a core skill for working at the company</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Codex improves itself: it runs its own test suite, runs improvement tasks overnight, and during team meetings it takes actions on topics discussed</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Google: AI widespread. </span></strong><span>Gemini is not as capable at coding as Claude or Codex, as acknowledged by Google’s CEO, but it’s widely used companywide.
