Antithesis enables teams like Jane Street, Fly.io,  and the etcd community to use agents safely and ship better code, faster. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e3f52f76-c491-4ab3-a2df-1378b210b367?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span style="color: rgb(0, 0, 0);">Learn more</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>• </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0ce6678b-81cf-4dda-af12-01e664558b1a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">WorkOS</a></strong><span> – make your app and agents Enterprise Ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0ce6678b-81cf-4dda-af12-01e664558b1a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Get started.</a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>• </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2b14ef9-0cbb-42be-95c7-4293f9b6897e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">turbopuffer</a></strong><span> – a vector and full-text search engine built on object storage. It’s fast, cheap, and extremely scalable. The teams building the smartest AI products out there — Cursor, Notion, Cognition, Anthropic — they </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d2b14ef9-0cbb-42be-95c7-4293f9b6897e?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">all run on turbopuffer</a><span>.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><strong>In this episode</strong></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Robert Erez is a principal engineer at Octopus Deploy, and a longtime expert in CI/CD, deployment systems, and software delivery. Rob and I were also once colleagues on the Skype web team, working on large-scale deployments and release processes.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this episode of</span><em> The</em><span> </span><em>Pragmatic Engineer</em><span>, I sit down with Rob to discuss how teams deploy software safely and efficiently at scale. We cover Kubernetes, GitOps, platform engineering, progressive delivery, feature flags, cloud development environments, and the growing role of AI in CI/CD workflows. We also get into the tradeoffs in different deployment approaches, why self-hosted software still matters for some organizations, and the recent evolution of software delivery practices.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">Key observations on deployments and CI/CD from the conversation with Rob</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Here are 10 interesting takeaways from our chat:</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/c9ba451e-654c-49a4-95ed-97b607ff898d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/2x0eq5oDOJY" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>1. Roll forward, never backwards. </strong><span>When a system has state – which typically means it uses databases – then doing a rollback can leave the code talking to a schema that’s no longer in sync. Rob’s advice is to not treat a failure in v2 as a trip back to v1, but rather as a push to v3 with the fix in it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>2. GitOps isn’t actually about Git.</strong><span> None of the four pillars of GitOps – 1) declarative, 2) versioned and immutable, 3) pulled, not pushed, 4) continuously reconciled  – require Git, although Git can work under these constraints. Yet, the term  ‘GitOps’ has made the industry dogmatic about cramming </span><em>everything</em><span> into a repo – even things like secrets that absolutely shouldn’t be there!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>3. Continuous deployment can be overkill; continuous delivery is more practical. </strong><span>Shipping every single change to prod (continuous deployment) is not as necessary as many people think, Rob says, and there’s often more value in continuous delivery, where changes flow through testing and the deployment process itself is validated. With continuous delivery, you can decide whether to push to production automatically, or click a button once a week.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>4. Feature toggles are a better safety net than rollbacks.</strong><span> When something breaks in production, reaching for a toggle to switch a feature off enables you to “stop the bleeding” and then calmly diagnose an issue. Rolling back a feature flag is less nerve-jangling than scrambling to force a redeployment in the middle of the night!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>5. One problem with feature flags is that they’re addictive.</strong><span> On the other hand, the ease with which feature flags are added can create a hygiene crisis if they’re continuously added, but not removed. Treat feature-toggle cleanups like a form of gardening and “weed” rolled-out toggles from the codebase.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>6. A Git repo can be a bottleneck at scale.</strong><span> Rob mentions that some companies run thousands of independent Kubernetes clusters that pull state from a Git repository. But such clusters can get throttled by the repo, forcing them into workarounds. Pull-based GitOps doesn’t scale infinitely for free.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>7. A sizable number of major institutions remain on-prem – and this won’t change. </strong><span>Banks, other financial bodies, and governments, demand full control over their hardware, upgrades, and downtime. That’s why Rob expects this segment won’t move to cloud-based SaaS.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>8. Platform teams work at larger companies. </strong><span>These teams earn their keep in big organizations with multiple teams and projects because they offer ways of bringing sanity and focus.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>9. There’s a trend of ephemeral environments replacing test/staging environments. </strong><span>Companies used to have a few testers fighting over a handful of static test environments, but today, it’s trivial to spin up a full environment, per-feature branch, pre-merge. This is an “ephemeral” environment for evaluating that things work, which is then torn down once something is merged. It helps speed up the feedback process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>10. AI shifts the CI/CD calculus from speed to risk.</strong><span> Today, shaving ten minutes off the CI build-time matters because a long-running build blocks human devs. But this time saving will be insignificant when an AI agent writes most of the code and “babysits” a slow pipeline without context switching. Then, the new priority will be to reduce the risk of an AI agent shipping a bug to production, so it will make much more sense to run extra, more thorough, tests – and also even slower ones.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;">For two decades, Meta had a unique, high-performance engineering org; right up until around April of this year. For the first 20 years of the company’s existence, it had a “move-fast-and-break-things” culture, and in the early 2020s this shifted to a “move-fast-with-stable-infra” one. Engineers I know at the company were empowered to do good work, focus on impact, and to balance business interests with solid engineering.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But in the past few weeks, all that has changed, as if the leadership has been following detailed blueprints on how to demolish a proven, successful engineering culture in the most ruthlessly efficient way possible.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For the past few weeks, I’ve been </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9fa16a18-4caf-4672-9054-f597f8294b90?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">sharing</a><span> how bad things are inside the social media company for engineers in one of Silicon Valley’s most prestigious workplaces. In this article, we walk through what’s happened, and ask what’s going through the minds of leadership who are reducing software engineering there from </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ede80667-8416-4522-9609-fb94e61936bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">the profit center</a><span> that it was between 2004 until very recently, to the disdained cost center that it has become in just a few weeks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We cover:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Meta’s pre-AI engineering culture</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Investing in AI and pressing engineers to always use it</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Core engineering folks feel treated like trash</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Most embarrassing-ever outage</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Internal mess</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Self-inflicted wounds</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Is it just Meta, or are other companies also acting irrationally?</p></li></ol><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Meta’s pre-AI engineering culture</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’d split Meta’s engineering culture into two eras: “move fast and break things”, and then “move fast with stable infra.”</p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);">“Move fast and break things”</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the 2010s, Facebook’s unconventional engineering culture had grown somewhat legendary in the tech industry, as the company went against conventional best practices and succeeded massively.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In 2012, when Facebook hit the billion-users landmark, the company produced a small physical book about its culture which was placed on employees’ desks. Presented with retro propaganda design, it was dubbed the “little red book”, co-opting the name of a famous volume of the thoughts of Chairman Mao, (1964).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">At around 70 pages long, Facebook’s version codified its engineering culture: speed, fearlessness, taking ownership, and thinking outside of the calc(1.375em * 1);">“Move fast with stable infra” culture</h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In 2022, I did what is one of the longest deepdives we’ve published on the topic of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6c260391-93c1-45d5-8890-4a627be97019?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">Meta’s engineering culture</a><span>. By then, things had evolved, and much of any former recklessness was gone, replaced by the principle of moving fast, but with stable infra. Here’s how I described Meta’s engineering culture then:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong>The culture is incredibly engineering-centric: much more than most of Big Tech. </strong><span>This might come from Mark Zuckerberg being an engineer himself, or because much of the innovation in the early days of Facebook came from engineers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Focus on individual impact.</strong><span> Impact has been the bread and butter of the focus at Facebook. This is very true since the early days, and the focus on generating impact remains.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One detail in common with most Big Tech firms is that both the engineering culture and general culture focus so much on individual impact. This results in some people focusing on short-term, measurable wins and assuming that teamwork and split wins between groups might be less rewarded.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>The lack of rigid processes.</strong><span> Facebook seems to have the least amount of processes or standardization across all of Big Tech. Don’t even try to compare it to</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9237df80-f515-432d-80e4-96a76e21ded8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"> Amazon’s engineering culture</a><span> and the countless formal processes there. But even compared to companies like Google, Microsoft or Uber, Facebook’s processes are much looser. Most of this comes from the engineering-centric nature of the company and engineers disliking processes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Surprisingly little emphasis on testing, documentation or code comments.</strong><span> You’ll find shockingly little automated testing and documentation at Facebook, compared to the rest of Big Tech. Inline code comments are also very rare.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>A founder-engineer driven company. </strong><span>Facebook is one of the few Big Tech firms whose founder is an engineer, and still is the CEO. Netflix is the other one where founder and co-CEO Reed Hastings was also a software engineer before starting the company. Amazon was the other example of this until recently, but it’s not the case at Google or Apple. There are good examples of smaller companies like Cloudflare, but they’re all younger than Facebook.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Bootcamp</strong><span>. A unique onboarding process, unlike what any other Big Tech firms offer. We cover this more in the</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a9fd3806-076b-4987-9253-45d6e699388d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"> Bootcamp & onboarding section.</a><span>”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, Facebook, as a product, has one of the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/885178de-034f-4274-88d3-9088b8076c7c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">most sophisticated auto rollout systems</a><span> in the industry. Instagram has a battle-tested infrastructure where it was almost trivial </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e7536c4d-5e3a-4738-83ec-cc2208aaa3e6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">to launch a new social network (Threads)</a><span> with 100 million users served in its first week.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Engineers whom I knew inside the company are capable, motivated, and product-minded, and their work was appreciated. CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, was influential: he personally coded the first version of Facebook, had stayed close to engineering, and valued software engineers very much. Engineers there felt they were working inside a profit center.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">2. Investing in AI and pressing engineers to always use it</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Meta has been the only company among the big five of Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, and itself not to own a hardware platform or operating system. Apple has the iPhone, iPad and Macs, Google has Android, ChromeOS and Pixel phones, Microsoft has Windows, and Amazon has the Kindle.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Stepping back, it looks as though the Mark Zuckerberg of today has resolved not to miss a platform opportunity, after the company failed to build its own mobile OS or mobile phone during the 2010s.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is one reason for investing so much in virtual reality (VR) with Oculus, and in augmented reality with the Meta Glasses. Facebook changed its name to Meta in 2021, back when it looked like VR – and the metaverse – could be massive. Billions was spent on ensuring Meta would be the market leader in this space. But once again, VR didn’t go mainstream; since the end of the pandemic, popular interest in the segment has died down considerably.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">When it became clear that AI would become a mega-trend in 2022, Zuckerberg didn’t miss it: he assembled the internal FAIR group (Fundamental AI Research team), and released a series of open-weight AI models:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Llama 1</strong><span>: released in Feb 2023, three months after ChatGPT</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Llama 2</strong><span>: in June 2023</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Llama 3</strong><span>: in April 2024. This model was Meta’s most competitive LLM of all, and gained momentum in adoption across the industry</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Llama 4</strong><span>: in April 2025. This model was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bc9a5392-e21a-49fd-9dbf-f69a7fdcebb4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">deeply disappointing</a></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>In June that year, Meta acquired Scale AI to reboot its AI efforts </strong><span>for a whopping $14.8B, and brought Scale AI’s CEO, Alexandr Wang to take over Meta’s AI strategy. The acquisition of Chinese startup Manus AI for $2B is currently in question after China </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0658b4dd-6beb-4a89-90f6-b78f959794dc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">blocked</a><span> the deal from being completed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Based on the investment made into Scale AI, it’s pretty clear that Meta – and Zuckerberg – is determined to build a state-of-the-art LLM that can be competitive with the latest versions of Claude and ChatGPT. But Meta has to start pretty much from scratch, and it’s up to Alexandr Wang to deliver.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Scale AI brings in a very specific kind of expertise to Meta, as one of the best in the industry in:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Training data and labeling: </strong><span>Scale started, and is still best known, as a provider of high-quality labeled datasets for machine learning and AI training, including code, text, image, video, etc.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>RLHF and fine-tuning: </strong><span>A RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) flow which Scale runs, where people give feedback for foundation models, as a “human in the loop” data engine that many leading AI labs use to create better LLMs.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Wang seems to have a very broad reign to do what he has been an expert in: creating training data, doing data labeling and RLHF. This is being pulled off with the labor of Meta’s engineering workforce, and by surveilling it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Problem #1: Tracking keystrokes and mouse clicks, with no option to opt out. </strong><span>In late April, Meta told engineers they were being enrolled into a system that tracks every keystroke and click, to produce training data for Meta’s new AI. There’s no way to opt out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Needless to say, this is invasive and raises privacy questions: If you log into your personal bank account, does the tool track you? What about when you’re writing a personal email, or responding to a personal call? Meta held no consultation and there are no workarounds; just a top-down decision being pushed through.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This month, Reuters </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/46c770f4-a87c-4e7e-bfd2-8b9cd5d11f62?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reported</a><span> that people’s concerns there are finally being heard:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Meta is dialing back elements of its plan to collect employee mouse movements, keystrokes and other actions for use as AI ​training data, it said in an internal memo on Tuesday, following weeks ​of angry pushback from staffers.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">New controls will allow employees to pause ⁠the data collection for up to 30 minutes at a time and ​request exemptions from the initiative, according to the memo, authored by Stephane Kasriel, ​a vice president in Meta’s AI model-building Superintelligence Labs unit.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">From talking with current Meta engineers, I understand the logging system has not been rolled out in the UK due to data protection regulation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Problem #2: 30-50% of engineers on core teams have been forcefully reassigned to data labeling </strong><span>and RLHF, upsetting folks even more.</span><strong> </strong><span>Also starting in late April, product engineering teams received a mandate from above, whereby 30-50% of engineers were to leave the team and join the ADO org (Agent Data Optimisation).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>“Forceful” reassignment is very relevant here because of Meta’s traditional engineering culture. </strong><span>Between its founding in 2004 and until last year, Meta gave engineers autonomy to choose where they work and what they work on. This was structural to how the company worked:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Engineers were not hired for a specific team (save for at the Staff+, levels, in some cases). They were hired to the company</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">During a 6-week bootcamp, new hires got familiar with Meta’s engineering culture and chose a team</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Team matching meant talking with multiple teams who had headcount, doing small work with them, and finding a match</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Internal transfers were easy, and often initiated by engineers</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Team selection via bootcamp started to die down in around 2024, but any Meta engineer with at least two years’ tenure knows that previously they chose what to work on, and of course, could pick the most impactful thing to work on. And then, out of the blue, they’re assigned to a division where the impact is not clear, the work is menial, and doing it too long will surely hurt their career prospects.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Infrastructure and security teams were hit especially hard by reassignments. </strong><span>I talked with several engineers in infra orgs, who had 30-50% of their teams drafted into the ADO org. And in some cases, it was the best engineers who left.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">One engineer told me that the whole situation feels like the movie, The Hunger Games, when tributes are randomly selected and then removed from their environment, to something completely different. Except, at Meta, many more folks are being affected, with between three and five from a 10-person team going from building products used by hundreds of millions, to giving human feedback on AI-generated GitHub repos, over and over. So, a wider impact than in the Hunger Games, but with less drastic consequences.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Around 6,500 people are in the ADO org, more than at OpenAI and Anthropic. </strong><span>Roughly four to five thousand of these are software engineers. Meta has around 25,000 engineers, meaning that one in every 5-6 software engineers may now find themselves doing data labeling full time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">As you can imagine, people are actively open to new positions, and nobody is updating their job title on LinkedIn and elsewhere to “data labeling at Meta.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I’ve spoken with people in this role and they don’t like doing it, and feel upset about the top-down decision making. The silver lining is that they still have a job, have retained their salary, and were not part of layoffs. They still have time to leave Meta for something that pays comparably and is not a data labeling job.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">3. Core engineering folks feel treated like trash</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Problem #3: a month-long waiting game, stoking fear across the company. </strong><span>On 20 April, Reuters </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d61c1788-780f-4150-9711-5d01bd2bc3a1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">reported</a><span> that Meta planned to lay off 10% of staff in a month’s time, and Meta confirmed the news, meaning there was a period of four weeks when everyone knew that they could be unemployed very soon.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Forced reassignments to data labeling started to happen. As I covered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9fa16a18-4caf-4672-9054-f597f8294b90?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">at the time:</a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Understandably, there are mixed feelings about this redeployment [to data labeling], with layoffs coming soon. On Wednesday, 20 May, Meta will announce layoffs. Perhaps those moved to do data labeling could actually be “safer” than colleagues on product teams. Of course, this is speculation, but it would be cruel if Meta cut devs reassigned to data labeling.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Problem #4: Performance review is hyper-aggressive at Meta, so devs optimize all metrics. </strong><span>The internal performance review process, PSC (Performance Summary Cycle), is very stringent, compared to Google and Apple, I’ve learned. Managers inside Meta “fight” over the pay packets of their employees, which involves “knocking down” the packet of engineers on other teams, so their direct reports are ranked higher. It’s common to weaponize metrics in this process – be that business impact, the number of code reviews, number of lines of code written, pre-AI (see </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e2c47a89-20ef-4273-8c12-032dc815f527?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">our Coding Machine archetype podcast</a><span> on this.)</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Quotas are handed down to managers for the splits of the workforce to be put in each ‘bucket’, and the internal politics gets heated as managers try to get their reports into higher buckets.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After a few years, engineers at Meta learn that the best way to not get a bad PSC rating is to have all metrics – impact, code committed, and other numbers – higher than their peers’ are. </span><em><span>Learn more about </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9e85219c-7264-44ee-bd43-765486ea8942?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">the internal politics of performance calibrations.</a></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Problem #5: tokens are measured as part of perf, so devs aggressively optimize for it. </strong><span>When layoffs were confirmed, engineers also learned that managers shall inspect token count during perf reviews. This raised worries that those with low token counts might be marked as underperformers and dismissed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, what is the natural reaction to this as an engineer at Meta? They started using AI tools for the sake of generating more tokens. This happened while Meta had an internal token leaderboard, encouraging tokenmaxxing. As I wrote </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/73feddd2-8589-42d5-bfa1-e69861153ac6?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">on 16 April:</a></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“As per The Information, Meta employees </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ffc6abfa-5e06-4be7-8d4e-787be8d3f56a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">used</a><span> a total of 60.2 trillion AI tokens (!!) in 30 days. If this was charged at Anthropic’s API prices, it would cost $900M. Of course, Meta is likely purchasing tokens at a discount, but that could still come in at $100M+ – in large part from senseless “tokenmaxxing”.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>The biggest problem: people stop caring about real work and focus on performative work. </strong><span>Let’s check the four ingredients that Meta’s leadership has decided to introduce to their workplace:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Tracking the keyboards and mouse clicks of all engineers, where legally possible</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Reassign a good chunk of engineers to fulltime data labeling</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Let staff know that 10% of them will be laid off</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Have a culture where devs optimize for any and all metrics measured during PSC</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Measure token usage as part of PSC</p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Shake this mix up well, and what do you get? Two things:</p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Everyone overuses AI to boost their personal stats. </strong><span>An engineering workforce that pretends to work with as much AI, and as little human input, as possible. It’s a strange incentive where an outage caused by a failure to review code properly is not grounds for dismissal, but writing code by hand – instead of having an AI agent write it – could cost you your job</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong>Every longer-tenured engineer is seeking a new job, or at least considering it.</strong><span> Those who have been around at Meta longer term have seen enough. Let me describe this visually:</span></p></li></ol><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 visualised</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">To its credit, Meta has given out generous retention equity packages to several engineers considered key on the remaining teams. These packages make it harder to get matching compensation elsewhere. Still, I talked to one engineer who got an equity top-up, and said that this approach helped him decide to leave as soon as possible because he feels bitter about the lack of autonomy and having no control over things.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">4. Most embarrassing-ever outage</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Meta’s core infra and security teams have suddenly found themselves severely understaffed. Most folks are pushing AI-generated code merged with AI-only reviews, without paying much attention to quality. After all, they’re dealing with the possibility of unemployment, while firefighting to operate a team without its best engineers whose headcount has been cut in half, all with the knowledge that AI usage could affect their own job security.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Two weeks ago, on 30 May, the most embarrassing outage in Meta’s history happened. </strong><span>Here’s software engineer Siddharth Sundharam’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/532afc9d-300b-4615-92cf-66498338a431?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">summary</a><span> (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Yesterday, a slew of Instagram accounts, including some high profile ones like the Obama White House account, seemingly got hacked.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Look, I’m no spring chicken. I’ve spent almost a decade and a half identifying vulnerabilities and exploits at unicorn scale, but this is hands down the most unserious, “almost too stupid to be true” of them all.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The Takeover Flow:</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Step 01: Faking the Location & Initiating Support. All the attacker needs to kick this off is your account username. Then, they hop on a VPN or proxy close to your city so Instagram’s security algorithms don’t suspect a thing. (You can quite easily get this from your public profile or “About” section or a hundred other ways.) Once it looks like the request is coming from the correct region, they tell the Meta support AI that the account is hacked and ask it to send the verification codes to an arbitrary email address they control.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Step 02: That’s It. Really, that’s it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>The first proper zero auth password reset I’ve seen in production.</strong><span> There appears to be no additional check as to whether the email being given is actually something the user has used before. Once the AI sends the security code to the attacker’s email, the attacker passes it right back to complete the verification. The platform hands over a fresh password reset link, granting full ownership to the attacker.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is a security breach in which Meta left its extra-secure, reinforced front door unlocked, so that anyone could come in, and there was no alarm to notify anybody when it happened! It seemed Meta only noticed when users started reporting it on social media!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>From talking with folks inside Meta, I’ve learned that AI was at the heart of this outage. </strong><span>AI-generated, AI-reviewed code, and security teams being gutted were together the cause of this beyond-embarrassing incident. I poked around, and here’s what I gathered:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Instagram’s Trust and Safety Team lost around 50% of its staff to data labeling and layoffs. Some of the most senior folks were drafted onto AI training tasks.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">AI-generated changes that saw no human input, just another AI code review, were very common during the last two months, across the codebase. The change that caused this outage looked like one of these</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Normally, the Trust and Safety team would be on top of monitoring and alerting of security breaches,  but it is currently in full disarray due to rapid, internal disorganization.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Meta’s Chief Security Officer resigned the very next day. </strong><span>The outage was resolved on Monday, 1 June, and an investigation started as part of the SEV process. On Tuesday, Meta’s Chief Information and Security Officer (CISO), Guy Rosen, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8b8afed4-bd08-4cb2-80bb-c06db7574f68?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">announced</a><span> his departure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Coincidence? I suspect not: the CISO might have stepped down if they warned against the Security org being gutted but were then ignored, and so no longer trusts leadership. I also imagine the CISO didn’t have the idea to move a good half of Instagram’s security team over to data labeling.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>As a note, the previously worst outage was all Meta services going down for seven hours </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6fe910fd-c7d0-46cb-a507-8938139547bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">in 2021</a><span>, due to a DNS / BGP configuration issue. It was a bad outage, but Meta handled the follow up well, in my opinion. After that 2021 outage, Meta </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/569d3ef7-27be-4181-8fd8-7d2964a1ff39?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">shared a postmortem and apology</a><span>. It has not done so for the latest Instagram account takeover outage.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">5. Internal mess</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Wired </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e5d3fe63-9cf6-4026-8578-28516e23e7e2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">shares more details</a><span> on just how bad the situation is inside Meta, right now:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“Someone interrupted a livestreamed, employee-only presentation at Meta earlier this week with an expletive-filled outburst about “being the company’s bitch,” according to a recording heard by WIRED. The individual then asked the people leading the call to write to a specific Meta AI executive and “tell him that he’s a piece of shit.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The incident, which took place on a call open to thousands of employees, reflects growing frustration inside the company’s Applied AI team, which was formed in March to support the work of AI researchers at Meta Superintelligence Labs. Three current employees tell WIRED there is widespread dissatisfaction with how Meta assembled the unit of about 6,500 engineers and product managers and the drudgework they allege they have been assigned to improve AI models.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“It’s literally the gulag,” one of the employees claims. “You have zero purpose in life all of a sudden, you barely interact with anyone, you just have these tasks every week.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s more: Meta’s Chief Product Officer, Chris Cox, reportedly admitted to staff that Meta’s upper leadership (the folks above him, meaning the C-level at Meta) created the mess. Also from Wired:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">During a meeting this week open to all employees at Instagram, Meta chief product officer Chris Cox addressed the “difficult” and “brutal” environment created by the “insanity of this company” in the past few months, according to a recording heard by WIRED. Cox applauded Instagram employees for launching features and serving around 2 billion users amid what he compared to “running a marathon in the middle of a hailstorm and then, like, your teammate gets replaced and then we’re recording you.”</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">“It’s like what the fuck,” he said, drawing laughs, before repeating himself. “It is like what the fuck.”</p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">6. Self-inflicted wounds</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">So, is there an ultimate source of the “insanity of this company”, as CPO Chris Cox put it? Engineers whom I talked to point the finger at two individuals: Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang. Zuckerberg has full control over the business, and has made the decisions to reallocate a good part of engineering folks to data labeling, to roll out tracking software, and to lay off 10% of staff when Meta achieved record revenue and profits. As the CEO, the buck clearly stops with him.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But it’s hard to unsee that – outside of layoffs – everything that Meta is doing is taken from the Scale AI playbook, and that surely comes from Wang:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Mandatory keystroke and mouse tracking to generate training data</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;">Forced data labeling with 4,500+ engineers is to generate high-quality RLHF, surely for Meta’s under-construction coding LLM</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Taking away the best engineers from the heart of the business is surely signed off by Mark Zuckerberg, believing that it is more important for Meta to train a coding AI than it is to operate its core business like Instagram, Facebook or Messenger reliably. Oh, did I mention that on Saturday (12 June) Facebook and Instagram </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e5ed3967-ca6b-4d04-8fe0-b417db8d07d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">had another SEV0</a><span>, that is, a full-on outage?</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before all this happened, Meta </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7fb6d676-9be9-4b09-983c-a88b72e10e00?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">was on track</a><span> to overtake Google as the world’s #1 ads business by the end of the year. But for some reason, Mark Zuckerberg decided that building a coding LLM is more important.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>Meta’s leadership is now trying to undo all the damage they have done. </strong><span>Wired reports that Meta CTO, Andrew Bosworth, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4efdb9ce-f2e4-4a8c-ab35-22349488ce82?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">admitted</a><span> to staff that the AI reorg was atrocious and committed to better communication in the future.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To me, it looks obvious that Zuckerberg doesn’t care how engineers feel about the massive changes, and that Bosworth likely ignored the chaos, all while engineers know for a fact that the next AI model matters more than they do to the business. Bosworth also said that employees will have access to AI coaching tools.</span><em> Very considerate, given the situation!</em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Based on all I’ve learned, Meta’s engineering culture is dead because leadership has made it clear that engineering at the company is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ede80667-8416-4522-9609-fb94e61936bc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">a cost center</a><span>.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table 20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em>Nice while it lasted</em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Needless to say, I hope my assessment is way off, but I’ve seen nothing yet from Mark Zuckerberg and Alexandr Wang – the two executives creating this current mess – to suggest it is.</span><em> There may be a short time period where, if major changes like data labeling assignments and staff tracking are undone, then things at Meta could return to normal. The longer the current conditions persist, the more tenured engineers will surely leave.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">7. Is it just Meta, or are other companies also acting irrationally?</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s tragic to see a technical founder at Meta so focused on AI that he neglects the engineers who built the heart of his company. But is Meta a one-off exception?</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Mitchell Hashimoto (creator of Ghostty, founder of HashiCorp) </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5dab457c-9ec0-42b4-96f0-be7a2e2f6bac?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">says</a><span> he is seeing similar behavior by other founders (emphasis mine:)</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong>I strongly believe there are entire companies right now under heavy “AI psychosis” and it’s impossible to have rational conversations about it with them.</strong><span> I can’t name any specific people because they include personal friends I deeply respect, but I worry about how this plays out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I lived through the great MTBF vs MTTR (mean-time-between-failure vs. mean-time-to-recovery) reckoning of infrastructure during the transition to cloud and cloud automation. All those arguments are rearing their ugly heads again but now it’s... the whole software development industry (maybe the whole world, really).</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s frightening, because ‘psychosis folks’ operate under an almost absolute “MTTR is all you need” mentality: “it’s fine to ship bugs because the agents will fix them so quickly and at a scale humans can’t do!” We learned in infrastructure that MTTR is great but you can’t yeet resilient systems entirely.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The main issue is I don’t even know how to bring this up to people I know personally, because bringing this topic up leads to immediate dismissals like “no no, it has full test coverage”, or “bug reports are going down” or something, which just don’t paint the whole picture.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We already learned this lesson once in infrastructure: you can automate yourself into a very resilient catastrophe machine. Systems can appear healthy by local metrics while globally becoming incomprehensible. Bug reports can go down while latent risk explodes. Test coverage can rise while semantic understanding falls. Changes happen so fast that nobody notices the underlying architecture decaying.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I worry.”</p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The takeover outage at Instagram was exactly like this: the engineering team dropped the quality bar for AI-generated and AI-reviewed code, probably expecting that they could recover quickly from failures. And they did indeed recover… after the damage was done, high-profile Instagram accounts were hacked, and the system was compromised, all very publicly.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Mitchell highlights the specific concern of founders over-estimating the capabilities of AI, and consequently casting aside sensible safeguards when shipping code to production.</p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);">Takeaways</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most of us probably have something to learn from the disastrous events at Meta caused by hyper-focus on AI to the exclusion of people who are the lifeblood of that company.</span><strong> </strong><span>In some good news, I’m hearing that in the UK, some of the 10% layoffs have suddenly been cancelled: at the end of the mandatory consultation period, several infra and security teams are learning that no engineers on their team will be let go, as originally expected.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Meta has a booming business, and is already a beneficiary of AI via increased ads revenue. Meanwhile, my Facebook feed is filled with fake, AI-generated videos, with hundreds of comments from bots and people who seemingly don’t realize it’s AI. It all seems like just more content for Meta to show ads next to.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And yet, despite business booming, Meta’s leadership has gone on a crusade to inflict the most damage possible on its engineering org. Apparently, they’re now learning that most of it was pointless.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong>If you’re in a leadership position and feeling the temptation to make drastic org changes for AI-related reasons, take a deep breath and see where it left Meta. </strong><span>Meanwhile, If you’re an engineer at a company whose leadership is over-indexing on AI, consider forwarding this article as additional context.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re hiring standout engineers who are extremely hands-on with AI, then it’s never been easier to get talent from Meta, than right now. Every engineer I know at the company is an extremely early adopter of AI, and knows how to build products and AI infra. These folks have soured on the company and its leadership. Meta’s loss of talent will be the gain of other startups and the rest of Big Tech; it’s one benefit of AI that’s probably a bit unexpected – not least of all by Meta!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;">It seems like the old mantra of “move fast and break things” has now extended to Meta’s engineering org itself, with the company’s rush to over-invest in AI, so it will avoid missing the latest mega-trend in the tech industry.</p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re on the free list for </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIwMjMwNzIzNiwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjp0cnVlLCJ1IjoxOTMwNDMxNDgsImlhdCI6MTc4MTYyNzU2MiwiZXhwIjoyMDk3MjAzNTYyLCJpc3MiOiJwdWItMCIsInN1YiI6ImxpbmstcmVkaXJlY3QifQ.oEDhxwMoXkKJgtSiK1go42t44DCG6gw7uPZybaajGCQ?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em><span>. rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In December 2024, an AI lab called DeepSeek released a 671-billion-parameter language model along with a technical report describing exactly how they built it. Six months later, a different team called Moonshot AI used that report as a starting point. They scaled the design to a trillion parameters, ran into a training instability problem that emerged at that scale, invented a new optimizer to solve it, and shipped their own model. Eight months after that, a third team called Zhipu AI integrated a different DeepSeek innovation into their architecture and contributed a new training framework of their own.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">These three teams work for different organizations. However, they were indirectly collaborating in public, through model releases where each company was learning from what its predecessors had done before. This has been made possible by the rise of open-weight models, where even competitors get to learn from each other. The pace of that kind of collaboration has changed over the past eighteen months, and the reasons trace back to the architecture and training choices these teams made in the open.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In this article, we will look at how open-weight models have transformed the AI landscape.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared </em><span>details</span><em> from various sources. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify">Open Weight vs Closed Weight</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Every modern large language model has two important things behind it:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The first is the trained parameters, which are the numbers, often hundreds of billions of them, that the model learned during training. The parameters are what make the model “know” things.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The second is everything that produced those parameters, including the training data and the training code.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">A closed-weight model is one that the company keeps behind an API. The user sends some text to the official API endpoint, the company’s servers run the model on their hardware, and a response comes back. The parameters stay with the organization, and running the model on personal hardware or adjusting it for a specific task remains out of reach.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">An open-weight model is one where the company has published the trained parameters. Anyone can download them, run the model on their own hardware, and adjust it for their own data. The training data and the full training code, however, usually stay private.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The term is “open weight” rather than “open source” for this reason.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In traditional software, “open source” means the full source code is available to inspect and reproduce. Most AI models marketed as open source are actually open weight, where the trained model is public, while the process that produced it remains closed. This distinction matters because the published weights, paired with detailed technical reports, are what allow other teams to study a design and build on top of it.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Different open-weight models also use different licenses, ranging from very permissive ones like MIT and Apache 2.0 to custom licenses with specific commercial restrictions, so the practical freedoms vary across the ecosystem.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below that shows the difference between accessing a closed-weight model and an open-weight model:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify">The MoE Architecture</h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Every major open-weight LLM released at the frontier in 2025 and 2026 shares the same architectural skeleton. It is called a Mixture-of-Experts transformer, or MoE for short.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">Modern LLMs are built from stacked “blocks.” Each block has two main parts, an attention layer that figures out which previous words matter for the next one, and a feed-forward layer that does the actual computation.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">In a regular (”dense”) model, every parameter activates for every word the model processes. Adding more parameters to make a smarter model means the cost of running it scales linearly with that count. With hundreds of billions of parameters, this becomes impractical.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">MoE solves this by replacing the single feed-forward layer in each block with several smaller “expert” sub-networks, plus a small routing component that picks which experts to use for each word. The model can store knowledge across many experts while only computing a few of them per word.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">This is why two numbers matter for every MoE model:</p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The first is total parameters, which represent the model’s full memory footprint and knowledge capacity.</p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify">The second is the active parameters, which represent how much of the model actually computes per word. Active parameters drive inference speed and per-query cost.</p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">DeepSeek V3, for example, has 671 billion total parameters but only 37 billion active per word. Kimi K2 has a trillion total, but 32 billion active. Qwen3 has 235 billion total and 22 billion active. When comparing the cost of running these models, the active counts are what matter, rather than the totals. A trillion-parameter model and a 235-billion-parameter model can cost roughly the same per query if their active counts are similar.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">See the diagram below that shows how an MoE block works:</p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: justify">Beginners often assume that experts in MoE specialize by topic, with a math expert, a code expert, and so on. The reality differs from that picture. The router picks experts per word, rather than per question, and the patterns experts specialize in are mostly outside human interpretation. The routing is fine-grained, and a single sentence will pass through many different combinations of experts as it generates.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify">The MoE architecture explains why every frontier open-weight team is using roughly the same approach. The interesting differences lie in the design choices teams make inside that design approach, and three places are where those choices show up most clearly.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height:
